prompts.assessment:
# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

NCVS Instrument Redesign

Description

 

BJS successfully transitioned to the redesigned NCVS instrument in 2025. Estimated data release timelines will be developed following the completion of data processing and data review procedures by the U.S. Census Bureau and BJS.


Overview of the NCVS Instrument Redesign 

The Bureau of Justice Statistics (BJS) last redesigned the National Crime Victimization Survey (NCVS) in 1992. Much has changed since that time, both in the nature of crime and in the public’s willingness to participate in surveys. As such, BJS initiated a multiyear effort to improve the efficiency, reliability, and utility of the NCVS. The effort had three main goals:

  • modernize the organization and content of the NCVS instrument
  • increase the quality of information collected and efficiency of the instrument flow
  • improve the measurement and classification of crime.

BJS is redesigning the entire survey instrument, which includes a household roster, victimization screener, and detailed crime incident report (CIR). During the research and testing phase of the redesign effort, BJS tested the revised instrument using multiple rounds of interviews with respondents that focused on comprehension of the questions and navigation through the instrument. BJS also tested data collection field procedures through a small-scale pilot test. The results of the testing informed the design of a new NCVS instrument that was assessed through a large-scale national field test. For additional information, see National Crime Victimization Survey Redesign Field Test Topline Report: Comparing Condition 1 and Condition 2 by Interleaving Treatment.

Highlights of the New NCVS Survey Instrument

The new NCVS instrument retains the two-stage measurement approach of the current instrument for the screening and classification of criminal victimization. It is more conversational in style and promotes recall by asking respondents to consider each subset of examples or probes separately. The new instrument also improves measurement of victimization and incident characteristics. For additional information, see Update on the NCVS Instrument Redesign.

Victimization screener updates include—

  • separating screening probes into shorter examples with yes/no responses in each screener series
  • revising probe contents
  • using more behaviorally specific language and expanding the screening probes for rape or sexual assault
  • adding vandalism as a crime screener.

Crime incident report updates include—

  • improving the use of victimization screener responses to drive questions asked in the CIR
  • revising items to improve measurement of key NCVS concepts (i.e., incident location and presence of respondent during incident)
  • increasing information collected about rape or sexual assault incidents
  • expanding measures of victim experiences, including use of victim services, satisfaction with police response, and consequences of victimization.

The new instrument will also include two new periodic modules:

  • The Police Performance module measures the types of contact with police and opinions about police performance.
  • The Community Safety module measures indicators of public perceptions of community issues related to crime and neighborhood safety.

 

The NCVS Instrument Redesign Timeline

BJS recently completed Phase 1 – Research and Testing, which culminated in the assessment of the redesigned instrument through a large-scale national field test. BJS, in collaboration with the U.S. Census Bureau, which carries out the NCVS data collection, will next initiate Phase 2 – Implementation.

The implementation phase includes instrument programming, instrument testing, and a small-scale pilot test to ensure that all data collection processes work correctly and meet statistical standards. To maintain the ability to report criminal victimization data during the phase-in of the new NCVS instrument, BJS will employ a split-sample design. For more information, see Update on the NCVS I

#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: National Crime Victimization Survey (NCVS)
Description: The National Crime Victimization Survey (NCVS) is the nation's primary source of information on criminal victimization. Each year, data are obtained from a nationally representative sample of about 240,000 persons in about 150,000 households. Persons are interviewed on the frequency, characteristics, and consequences of criminal victimization in the United States.
URL: https://bjs.ojp.gov/data-collection/ncvs

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

I'll research the National Crime Victimization Survey comprehensively. Let me start with several searches.Good start. Let me dig deeper into the timeline/history, data access, and usage.The timeline page is mostly an image. Let me search for more specific details on supplements, users/benefits, limitations, and analysis tools.I have solid material. Let me do two final searches on the analysis tools/subnational program and the ongoing instrument redesign.Let me fetch the instrument redesign page and the subnational program page directly.# National Crime Victimization Survey (NCVS) — Research Report

## Verification of Your Description

Your information is **accurate**. The title, description, and URL match the Bureau of Justice Statistics (BJS) exactly. The current NCVS data collection page (bjs.ojp.gov/data-collection/ncvs) confirms the survey interviews roughly 240,000 persons age 12 or older in about 150,000 households annually. A few useful nuances worth adding: the Census Bureau (not BJS staff) conducts the interviews; the sample size has varied over the decades (originally ~50,000 households/~100,000 persons); and annual estimates are based on victimizations experienced during a rolling 6-month reference period.

---

## 1. Publisher and Administrative Structure

| Role | Organization |
|---|---|
| **Sponsor / statistical agency** | Bureau of Justice Statistics (BJS), Office of Justice Programs (OJP), U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) |
| **Data collector (interviewer agency)** | U.S. Census Bureau, under an interagency agreement with BJS |
| **Data archive / distributor** | National Archive of Criminal Justice Data (NACJD) at ICPSR, University of Michigan |
| **Catalog listing** | Data.gov (listed under Department of Justice) |

BJS is one of the U.S. government's principal federal statistical agencies. The NCVS is its flagship collection and historically one of the largest ongoing surveys in the federal statistical system. Only Census employees sworn to preserve confidentiality (under Title 13, U.S. Code) may see completed questionnaires.

## 2. Legal Authority and Mandate

- **Authorizing statute**: The Omnibus Crime Control and Safe Streets Act of 1968, as amended, authorizes BJS to "collect and analyze information concerning criminal victimization, including crimes against the elderly, and civil disputes," and to produce data serving as a "continuous and comparable national social indication of the prevalence, incidence, rates, extent, distribution, and attributes of crime." The operative citation today is **34 U.S.C. § 10132** (formerly 42 U.S.C. § 3732, before the 2017 editorial reclassification of Title 42 provisions into Title 34).
- **BJS itself** was created by the Justice Systems Improvement Act of 1979 (as a successor to the Law Enforcement Assistance Administration's statistics division), and the survey transferred to BJS in December 1979.
- **Supplemental mandates**: Specific legislation has added NCVS content over time — e.g., the 1994 Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act's directive to acquire data on use of excessive force by police led to the **Police-Public Contact Survey (PPCS)** supplement; the Violence Against Women Act (VAWA) directed improved measurement of domestic violence.
- **Confidentiality**: Responses are protected under Title 13 (Census) and BJS's own confidentiality statutes; data are used for statistical purposes only.

## 3. History and Evolution

- **Origins (1960s)**: The President's Commission on Law Enforcement and Administration of Justice (mid-1960s) and Census-sponsored conferences (1967–68) recommended a national victimization survey after pilot studies in Washington DC, Baltimore, San Jose, and Dayton (1970–71) showed police-recorded statistics badly undercounted crime — the so-called **"dark figure of crime."**
- **1972–73**: The Law Enforcement Assistance Administration (LEAA) launched the **National Crime Survey (NCS)** in July 1972 (first full national data for 1973). The original program had three components: the National Crime Panel (the survivor, today's NCVS), a Commercial Victimization Survey (dropped in 1977 for budget reasons), and city-level surveys (discontinued).
- **1979**: Transferred from LEAA to the newly created BJS.
- **1975–1985**: A National Academy of Sciences review prompted a major redesign research consortium.
- **1986**: Non-rate-affecting changes to the incident report introduced.
- **1992–93**: The major redesign phased in (new screener questions, improved recall cues, better measurement of sexual assault and domestic violence, CATI); the survey was renamed the **National Crime Victimization Survey (NCVS)**. First fully redesigned annual estimates were published for 1993, which is why long-run trend series often begin in 1993.
- **2000s–2010s**: Periodic sample redesigns tied to each decennial census; a 2012 methodological change counting series victimizations up to 10 incidents (previously counted as one in published estimates); a 2016 sample redesign supporting subnational estimation; new demographic items added (veteran status, citizenship, sexual orientation and gender identity, disability).
- **2020**: COVID-19 disrupted fieldwork, reducing response rates and sample yields — an important caveat for 2020–2021 estimates.
- **2023**: BJS celebrated the survey's 50th anniversary.
- **2025**: BJS transitioned to a **newly redesigned NCVS instrument** — the first full instrument overhaul since 1992. Changes include shorter yes/no screener probes, behaviorally specific rape/sexual assault screening language, a vandalism screener, expanded measures of victim services use and satisfaction with police response, and two new periodic modules (Police Performance and Community Safety). A split-sample design is used to bridge old and new instruments. **Data users should expect a series break and should not naively splice pre- and post-redesign estimates.**

## 4. Methodology (What a Data Scientist Needs to Know)

- **Design**: Nationally representative, stratified, multistage cluster sample. Stage 1: primary sampling units (PSUs — large metros, counties, or county groups) selected once per decade after each census. Stage 2: addresses sampled annually (group quarters every 3 years).
- **Rotating panel**: Households stay in sample 3.5 years; eligible persons interviewed every 6 months for a total of **7 interviews**. If residents move, the *new* occupants at the address are interviewed. First interview is bounding (used to correct telescoping) and typically in person; later interviews by phone or in person.
- **Reference period**: Prior 6 months (excluding interview month). Crimes are classified by year of interview, not year of occurrence.
- **Instruments**: NCVS-500 Control Card (roster), NCVS-1 Basic Screen Questionnaire ("short-cue" screening questions), NCVS-2 Crime Incident Report (one per incident). Crime types are assigned by algorithm from incident attributes, not respondent labels — enabling uniform national classification despite varying state laws.
- **Crimes measured**: Nonfatal personal crimes (rape/sexual assault, robbery, aggravated and simple assault, personal larceny) and household property crimes (burglary/trespassing, motor vehicle theft, other theft) — **both reported and not reported to police**.
- **Series victimizations**: High-frequency repeat incidents the victim can't separate are documented once but weighted as the reported count up to a cap of 10 (since 2011/2012 methods change; ~4% of violent victimizations in 2024).
- **Weights and variance**: Person, household, and incident weights; complex design means analysts should use Taylor linearization, replicate weights, or BJS's generalized variance functions — naive simple-random-sample variance calculations will understate standard errors.
- **File structure**: Address, household, person, and incident record types (annual files), plus concatenated longitudinal files (currently 1992/1993 forward), plus an incident-level extract.

## 5. Scope Limitations and Known Criticisms

- **Exclusions**: Persons under 12; people experiencing homelessness; institutionalized populations (prisons, jails, nursing homes, hospitals); military personnel in barracks; crew of maritime vessels; U.S. citizens abroad; foreign visitors. Homicide is inherently unmeasurable by victim interview; arson, vandalism (until the 2025 redesign), kidnapping, crimes against businesses, and "victimless" crimes (drug possession, prostitution, etc.) are also out of scope.
- **Recall/response error**: Telescoping, memory decay, reluctance to disclose (especially sexual assault and intimate partner violence, historically cited as undercounted even after the 1992 redesign).
- **National-level focus**: Core design supports national estimates; subnational (state/local) estimates are a newer, partial product.
- **Complement, not competitor, to police data**: BJS and the FBI jointly publish comparisons (e.g., *The NCVS and NIBRS: A Complementary Picture of Crime*). NCVS captures unreported crime, simple assault, and threats; UCR/NIBRS capture homicide, commercial crime, and crimes against children under 12. The two series can diverge in any given year — a frequent source of political misinterpretation that advocates should be prepared to explain.
- **Response-rate pressure**: Like all federal household surveys, response rates have declined over time; the 2025 redesign explicitly addresses efficiency and participation.

## 6. Supplements (Topical Modules)

Administered to NCVS respondents immediately after the core interview, typically for 6 months, on rotating schedules:

| Supplement | Topic | Years fielded |
|---|---|---|
| **Identity Theft Supplement (ITS)** | Prevalence, impacts, reporting of identity theft (age 16+) | 2008, 2012, 2014, 2016, 2018, 2021 |
| **Police-Public Contact Survey (PPCS)** | Police contacts, traffic stops, use of force, satisfaction (age 16+) | 1996 (pilot), 1999, 2002, 2005, 2008, 2011, 2015, 2018, 2020, 2022 |
| **School Crime Supplement (SCS)** | School crime, bullying, safety (ages 12–18); co-sponsored with NCES, Dept. of Education | 1989, 1995, 1999, biennially 2001–2019, resumed 2022; next 2025 |
| **Supplemental Victimization Survey (SVS)** | Stalking victimization (age 16/18+) | 2006, 2016, 2019 |
| **Supplemental Fraud Survey (SFS)** | Seven types of personal financial fraud | Recent addition |

Earlier supplements covered topics like workplace violence. Supplement public-use files are archived at NACJD.

## 7. Data Access and Tools

1. **Public Use Files** — NACJD/ICPSR (free, no institutional affiliation required): annual and concatenated files in SAS, SPSS, Stata, R, and delimited ASCII, with codebooks and setup files. The full series from 1973 forward (including pre-redesign NCS files) is preserved here — the key resource for preservationists.
2. **NCVS Select Datasets via API** — a curated set of commonly used variables, concatenated 1993–present, for programmatic access.
3. **NCVS Victimization Analysis Tool (NVAT)** — BJS's online point-and-click tool for generating custom tables/trends without statistical software.
4. **Restricted Use Files** — accessible only through the Census Bureau's Federal Statistical Research Data Centers (FSRDCs) after an approved proposal; needed for most subnational geography and less-disclosed variables. (A Standard Application Process exists for restricted BJS data.)
5. **Publications**: The flagship annual bulletin *Criminal Victimization*, plus special reports (hate crime, intimate partner violence, firearm victimization, elderly victimization, identity theft, police contacts, school crime via the joint *Indicators of School Crime and Safety*), methodological documentation (e.g., *NCVS 2016 Technical Documentation*), and data.gov listings.

## 8. Typical Users

- **Congress and federal policymakers**: CRS reports and legislative debates on crime rely on NCVS; VAWA, VOCA, and anti-stalking/identity-theft legislation drew on NCVS evidence.
- **DOJ/OJP and the Office for Victims of Crime**: sizing the victim population for victim services planning.
- **State and local governments**: especially via the subnational program.
- **Academic researchers**: criminology, sociology, public health, economics — one of the most-used datasets in U.S. social science.
- **Victim advocates and policy activists**: documenting unreported crime, underuse of victim services, and disparities by race, ethnicity, disability, and sexual orientation/gender identity.
- **Journalists and the public**: annual NCVS vs. FBI UCR releases are a staple of national crime coverage.
- **International community**: the NCVS is the model for victimization surveys worldwide (e.g., the Crime Survey for England and Wales, ICVS).

## 9. Public Benefits

1. **Measures the "dark figure of crime"**: roughly half or more of violent victimizations are never reported to police; the NCVS is the only national statistical window into that hidden volume.
2. **Independent cross-check on police administrative data** — essential for public trust and for detecting reporting-driven artifacts in official statistics.
3. **Victim-centered detail**: consequences (injury, medical costs, lost work, emotional toll), victim-offender relationships, weapons, self-protective actions, reasons for non-reporting, and experiences with police and victim services — information no administrative system collects.
4. **Uniform national measurement** across 50 states with differing legal definitions, enabling a consistent 50-year time series.
5. **Equity measurement**: demographic richness allows analysis of disparate victimization burdens (e.g., persons with disabilities experience violent victimization at several times the rate of others).
6. **Informs funding and rights**: shapes allocation of billions in victim assistance and compensation and underpins landmark victim-protection laws.

## 10. Notes for Preservationists and Data Librarians

- **Continuity risk is the main preservation concern**: the 2025 instrument redesign will create a series break; preserving pre-2025 questionnaires, codebooks, and methodology reports alongside data is essential for interpretability.
- **The complete series (1973–present), including supplements, is archived at NACJD/ICPSR**, with persistent study numbers (e.g., ICPSR 38962 for the 2023 file; concatenated files like ICPSR 39273/38963). NACJD also preserves the NCS-era files and redesign documentation.
- **Legacy URL fragility**: older bjs.gov links have migrated to bjs.ojp.gov; older PDFs are preserved via OJP's NCJRS virtual library and digitization project — useful when primary links rot.
- **Documentation to capture**: NCVS-1/NCVS-2 instruments, control cards, technical documentation (2016 edition is the canonical recent one), methodology reports (e.g., the 2012 series-victimization methods report, NCJ 237308), and errata/data corrections pages.
- **Licensing**: U.S. government work; public-use files are freely downloadable, but users must agree to ICPSR terms (no re-identification attempts). Restricted files remain under FSRDC control and cannot be mirrored.

**Bottom line**: The NCVS is a 50+ year, statutorily mandated, BJS-sponsored/Census-administered panel survey that constitutes — alongside the FBI's UCR/NIBRS — one of the two pillars of U.S. national crime measurement. Its unique value is counting crime the justice system never sees. Its ongoing 2025 instrument redesign and the richness of its public-use archive make it both a high-value analytic resource and a meaningful preservation target.

## Research Summary

I researched the current state of the Bureau of Justice Statistics (BJS), the NCVS's Paperwork Reduction Act clearance history, FY 2025–2027 budget documents, Federal Register notices, and analyses from the American Statistical Association (ASA), Council on Criminal Justice, Brennan Center, APDU, and crime-data analysts. Key developments since January 2025:

1. **Executive Order 14168 (Jan 2025)** drove the removal of gender identity questions from the NCVS core instrument and School Crime Supplement (March–May 2025 nonsubstantive ICR changes, OMB 1121-0111 and 1121-0184). Census field representatives were instructed to skip the questions as early as Jan 31, 2025 — before OMB approval, which OMB/OIRA formally flagged as procedurally improper.
2. **The NCVS ICR was renewed** — OMB approved a revision on December 15, 2025, extending clearance through **December 31, 2028** (incorporating the 2020-census-based sample redesign) — but with a **~10% reduction in sampled housing units** and lower response/burden totals (157,439 vs. 180,831 responses).
3. **BJS lost an estimated 14% of staff since FY24** (ASA, *The Nation's Data at Risk 2025*), and the FY26 President's Budget Request cut BJS to ~$55.7M (≈8% purchasing-power loss from FY25); the FY27 request is $55.0M for the Research, Evaluation, and Statistics account, $10M below the FY25 enacted $65M.
4. **Core publication continued on time**: *Criminal Victimization, 2024* (the 52nd in the series) was released September 29, 2025. However, the promised companion estimates from the **2024 redesigned instrument** remain unreleased "at a later date."
5. Analysts (Jeff Asher, ASA, Council on Criminal Justice) have flagged NCVS as vulnerable because it costs ~$55M/yr — roughly BJS's entire budget — and DOGE has reportedly prioritized cutting data collections not explicitly required by statute.

---

## Category-by-Category Assessment

### 1. Historical Data Availability

**Evidence:**
- *No Known Issue*: The full NCVS series (1973–present) remains archived at NACJD/ICPSR with no reported file removals. *Criminal Victimization, 2024* and all prior annual reports remain on bjs.ojp.gov. The 2025 gender-identity changes were **prospective** (questionnaire revisions); previously collected data with SOGI variables have not been retroactively altered or withdrawn from the archive. The NCVS API and N-DASH dashboard remain live with 2024 legacy-instrument data.
- *Higher levels*: No evidence found of removed or altered historical files or elements.

**Assessment: No Known Issue.** Historical files remain accessible and unaltered at both BJS and NACJD. (Watch item: if the redesigned-instrument estimates are never released, 2024's split-sample year could become a permanently incomplete record — but that affects a new data product, not existing historical data.)

### 2. Future Data Availability

**Evidence:**
- *No Known Issue*: ICR renewed before expiration — OMB approval 12/15/2025, expiration now 12/31/2028. Data collection is continuous; the flagship annual report was published on its normal September schedule. Routine Federal Register notices (July 24 and Oct 2, 2025) show an orderly PRA process.
- *Moderate Risk*: The **2024 redesigned-instrument victimization estimates were intended for release but are delayed indefinitely** ("BJS plans to separately release…at a later date," with no date as of late 2025) — an intended publication delayed. The approved revision reduces the sample by ~10%, shrinking future collection scope. NCVS's annual cost ($55.1M) approximately equals BJS's entire budget, and FY26/FY27 requests are flat-to-down; credible analysts warn collection could be scaled back under budget or DOGE pressure.
- *High Risk*: Not met — no statutory deadline missed, no skipped cycle, ICR not expired.

**Assessment: Moderate Risk.** The core series is on schedule and clearance runs through 2028, but an intended data release is delayed without a date, the approved collection is smaller going forward, and the funding base is contracting.

### 3. Data Quality

**Evidence:**
- *High Risk (literal)*: Documented **reductions in granularity**: (a) gender identity demographic items removed from NCVS and SCS instruments in 2025, eliminating the ability to measure transgender people's victimization rates — APDU and public comments to OMB confirm this measurement capacity is lost; (b) ~10% sample reduction in the 2025–2028 clearance reduces precision for small subgroups and subnational estimates. The 2024–25 split-sample transition also creates a series break requiring bridging.
- *Moderate Risk*: Core crime-type measurement, timeliness, and frequency are maintained; the legacy 2024 estimates were produced normally. One could argue the reductions are bounded and thus "emerging" rather than realized.
- *No Known Issue*: Not supportable — actual (not merely potential) reductions have occurred.

**Assessment: High Risk** (with an important caveat). The rubric's High definition — "reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency" — is literally met by the removal of SOGI items and the sample cut. The caveat: these reductions are real but bounded; the survey's core measures of violent and property victimization continue at full frequency and timeliness. If your rubric intends "High" to signal broad degradation, Moderate would be defensible; on the plain text, the reductions have already happened.

### 4. Statutory Context

**Evidence:**
- *No Known Issue arguments*: The ICR explicitly lists **34 U.S.C. § 10132** (Justice System Improvement Act) as authorizing statute, which directs BJS to collect and analyze data on criminal victimization. Additionally, the **Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act (34 U.S.C. § 41305)** statutorily requires hate-crime statistics that BJS collects **through the NCVS** — OMB/White House Counsel expressly recognized this statutory hook in 2025. There is no substitute collection: UCR/NIBRS cannot measure unreported crime.
- *Moderate/High Risk arguments*: The statute authorizes victimization statistics broadly but does **not** mandate the NCVS by name, its sample size, or its frequency — as analyst Jeff Asher notes, "NCVS…is not statutorily required," making it a reported DOGE target category. The statutory mandate attaches to BJS's mission generally, not to this specific instrument.

**Assessment: Moderate Risk.** The NCVS is not explicitly required by name, but it is the sole vehicle for a statutorily required data product (hate crime statistics under § 41305) and the explicitly authorized core of BJS's victimization mandate, with no substitute collection. That fits the Moderate definition precisely; the "vague authorization + statutory-hook protection" combination cuts against both No Known Issue and High Risk.

### 5. Staffing and Funding

**Evidence:**
- *Moderate Risk (met)*: ASA estimates BJS lost **~14% of staff since FY24** (within the 10–39% band; note BJS is tiny — roughly 50–60 FTE — so this is ~8 people, far below the 500-person absolute thresholds). FY26 PBR ($55.7M) is ~6% below FY25 nominally and 8% in purchasing power; the FY27 request ($55.0M) is ~15% below the FY25 enacted $65M — straddling the 10–19% band depending on baseline. ASA rated BJS resources "WEAK," meaning the agency is "severely challenged" in meeting Evidence Act duties. The Census Bureau — the actual data collector — is also under hiring freeze and staffing strain, compounding risk. BJS has also faced a 42% nominal budget decline since FY2010 and has previously been forced to cut NCVS sample sizes for cost reasons.
- *High Risk*: Not clearly met — staffing loss is below 40%, budget cut is below 20% in most comparisons. Leadership: BJS has been led by an acting director (Kevin M. Scott) rather than a Senate-confirmed appointee; I found no confirmed removal of leadership in 2025, so the "leadership removed" trigger is not documented. (I was unable to complete a dedicated search on this point — treat leadership status as uncertain.)
- *No Known Issue*: Clearly not met given documented staffing losses and budget erosion.

**Assessment: Moderate Risk.** Staffing losses (~14%) and real-dollar budget contraction fall squarely in the Moderate bands, and the chronic underfunding of BJS (NCVS alone ≈ the agency's entire budget) makes the survey unusually exposed to any further cut.

### 6. Policy

**Evidence:**
- *High Risk (met)*: There is a documented **Presidential Action–driven ICR**: EO 14168 directly caused the March 2025 nonsubstantive change request (OIRA ref. 202503-1121-001) removing gender identity questions from the NCVS, with follow-on changes in May 2025 and parallel changes to the School Crime Supplement, Survey on Sexual Victimization, and Survey of Inmates in Local Jails. Census field staff were directed to skip questions even before OMB approval — an extraordinary intervention that OIRA formally rebuked. Separately, a January 2025 EO caused cancellation of the BJS-supported National Law Enforcement Accountability Database. These are squarely "significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities."
- *Moderate Risk*: Would apply if changes were merely proposed — but they were **implemented**.
- *Gone*: Not met — collection and publication continue.

**Assessment: High Risk.** An EO-driven ICR materially changed what the NCVS collects in 2025 — the literal definition of this rubric level. This also signals willingness to intervene in BJS collections, elevating the probability of further content changes (e.g., around hate-crime motivation items, which were paused and only reinstated after OMB/White House Counsel invoked the statutory requirement).

## Summary of Risk Levels

- **Historical Data Availability: No Known Issue**
- **Future Data Availability: Moderate Risk**
- **Data Quality: High Risk** *(bounded — core crime measures intact; granularity reduced via SOGI item removal and ~10% sample cut)*
- **Statutory Context: Moderate Risk**
- **Staffing and Funding: Moderate Risk**
- **Policy: High Risk**

**Overall interpretation**: The NCVS is not in imminent danger of termination — it is actively collected, freshly cleared through 2028, and publishing on schedule — but it has already sustained policy-driven content losses in 2025, operates on a budget that leaves zero margin, and sits in an agency flagged by the ASA as severely resource-challenged. For preservation purposes, the highest-priority items are: (1) pre-2025 instruments and data containing gender identity variables (now irreplaceable going forward); (2) 2024 split-sample legacy vs. redesigned instrument data and bridging documentation; and (3) current NACJD files, which remain the stable canonical archive even if the BJS website changes.
